messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mark has been a social worker for nearly thirty years, a career built on his capacity to enter chaotic situations and find a path forward. Now, at fifty-three, he finds his own world has become the one he can no longer navigate. The change began eight months ago, following a home visit to a new client. He remembers waiting in the narrow, dim apartment hallway, a delay that felt unusual at the time but now replays in his mind as a premonition. When the door finally opened, he was pulled inside. The assault happened quickly, brutally, in a small, cluttered bedroom with the door shut. The feeling of being overpowered in that confined space, the door a barrier to any possible escape, is the memory that has since dismantled his life.

In the weeks that followed, the event lived not as a coherent story but as a series of punishing sensory fragments. When he tries to remember it, to make sense of what happened, the same suffocating terror he felt in that room returns, a physical wave of cold dread that steals his breath. He has tried, on several occasions, to explain it to his wife, Sarah, but the words refuse to form. He knows what happened, he can see it behind his eyes, but language fails him. The attempt itself brings on an intense, hot shame that silences him completely, leaving him feeling hollowed out and pathetic. He has come to believe that being unable to speak about it is a profound personal failing, another layer of weakness.

His daily routines are now governed by a constant, humming sense of threat. Walking from his office to the parking garage has become a tactical mission. He is acutely aware of every person behind him, the sound of their footsteps seeming to quicken with his own. He finds himself stopping abruptly to pretend to tie a shoe or check his phone, just for the chance to look over his shoulder and confirm no one is following him. Unfamiliar places have become impossible. At work, he refuses any new cases that would require a home visit in a part of the city he doesn't know well. He tells his supervisor it’s a matter of efficiency, but in truth, he cannot bear the thought of walking into a building where he can’t anticipate the dangers. This has created a noticeable friction with his colleagues and a growing file of deferred cases on his desk.

To manage the intrusive memories, Mark has developed strategies that only seem to dig him deeper into his distress. He spends hours at night, long after Sarah is asleep, ruminating. He replays the assault not as it was, but as it could have been. In these fantasies, he is not frozen; he fights back, he overpowers his assailant, he escapes. He imagines tracking the man down, exacting a cold and satisfying revenge. These thoughts provide a fleeting sense of control, but they are exhausting and always leave him feeling more helpless than before. When the memories or the rage become too overwhelming, he tries to shove them down, to force them out of his mind by focusing intently on paperwork or a television show, but it’s like holding a beach ball underwater; the thoughts always surge back with greater force.

The world feels like it is closing in on him. He takes the stairs at his office building now, unable to tolerate the few seconds inside a sealed elevator. He feels a spike of panic in small, windowless meeting rooms. His marriage is strained by his silence, and his job, the bedrock of his identity, is becoming precarious. It was a final warning from his supervisor about his "unwillingness to engage with new client populations" that finally propelled him to seek help. He is terrified of losing his career, but what frightens him more is the chilling realization that he is losing himself. He has come to therapy with the fragile hope of finding the words he has lost, and perhaps, a way back to the man he used to be.
